debate_title: Compute governance as a lever for AI safety: export contr...

conflicts.point: Whether zero-knowledge cryptographic verification or other automated technical mechanisms can reliably enforce training compute limits without introducing prohibitive overhead or failing to capture software efficiency gains.

positions.stance: Zero-knowledge cryptographic validation allows training clusters to mathematically prove adherence to compute limits without exposing proprietary architectures or requiring expensive legal retainers.
Cryptographic verification fails because proofs can verify execution steps while remaining blind to semantic alignment and software efficiency multipliers that bypass raw hardware metrics.

conflicts.point: Whether physical infrastructure telemetry and static training compute ceilings effectively mitigate frontier security risks or merely entrench incumbent cloud providers through administrative moats.

positions.stance: Physical infrastructure metrics and mandatory telemetry anchors are necessary to prevent irreversible capability escalation in massive training runs, despite compliance frictions.
Permissionless open-source iteration and rapid scientific dissemination take priority, making any hardware-tied export controls an unacceptable form of central planning that causes preventable harm.

verdicts.conflict: Whether zero-knowledge cryptographic verification or other automated technical mechanisms can reliably enforce training compute limits without introducing prohibitive overhead or failing to capture software efficiency gains.
verdicts.rationale: Algorithmic efficiency techniques like quantization and FlashAttention are documented engineering realities that reduce hardware demands for training. The safety position relies on speculative cryptographic protocols that lack large-scale deployment proof for hardware enforcement.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Peer-reviewed deployment data showing zero-knowledge proofs successfully capturing runtime algorithmic efficiency gains on live training clusters would flip the verdict.

verdicts.conflict: Whether physical infrastructure telemetry and static training compute ceilings effectively mitigate frontier security risks or merely entrench incumbent cloud providers through administrative moats.
verdicts.rationale: Skeptics and accelerationists provide concrete evidence regarding legal compliance overhead and lobbying dynamics by large cloud providers. Safety advocates offer broad security goals but lack specific mechanisms to prevent static compute caps from acting as protectionist barriers.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical evidence demonstrating that small open-source developers easily absorb Bureau of Industry and Security compliance costs without market concentration would flip the verdict.
